body_markdown:
Sometimes we don’t need another project. We know better than to scroll through our favorite online marketplaces. Yet we sit down with a fresh cup of coffee and take a few minutes to daydream about what could be if we had the time and cash to buy that broken Ford tractor or that rusty hulk of[a vintage Kaiser](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1948-kaiser-special/) . Sometimes, the allure of what could be is just too strong, and we send a message to the seller proposing a meetup time, knowing full well that the message will require a trip to the bank we shouldn’t be making. I’m using “we” a lot here, because surely this experience is not unique to me.


The latest distraction to come across my screen was something I never thought I would own: The smallest version of a motorcycle, better known as a pocket bike, listed as a 1984 AJP Dandy. These are comical to ride as an adult, yet from the moment I saw it, I knew it was coming home with me. The listing title was clearly wrong—the platform forces you to pick a brand and model when creating a listing—but the photos captured me. The tiny fiberglass fairing simply had to be in my shop, even if purely for ornamental purposes.


It’s adorable.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Yet surprisingly well built.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The tiny little thing captured me from the first look.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I remember these pocket-bike motorcycles from my youth, when they were something of an annoyance. The same way electric motor–powered, bicycle-shaped objects are both aspirational and unavoidable for those of a certain age today, pocket bikes were the prize at the top of the pyramid-shaped candy-bar-selling scam most of my generation can recall from grade school. Those pocket bikes seemingly came out of nowhere and for no reason. As I found out, the early 2000s represent only the second wave of interest in these tiny things. The original wave was nearly a quarter century earlier, according to a[couple](https://magazine.cycleworld.com/article/1981/2/1/return-of-the-pocket-bike)[articles](https://davestestsandarticles.weebly.com/uploads/4/8/4/5/4845046/cgaug82dandymr30.pdf) I found shortly after the listing for this machine, as both my brain and my fingers tried to move faster than Google search to figure out what exactly I was looking at.


This example was complete, and it also had something classic about it that modern ones don’t. The fiberglass fairing was both inoffensively shaped and present. So many of the cheap pocket bikes are only sold once they stop running and after half of their parts have been lost behind a shed in the backyard. I don’t know what it says about me, but complete seems to be the most valuable thing in my brain when shopping for old vehicles.


A message was sent. A meeting was scheduled. Cash was exchanged.


The chassis is well built, if quite simple.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


These Bridgestone Racing have seen better days, but are likely original.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


A disc brake on the rear keeps speeds in check.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


What came home is a Kendee Dandy MR-30, or at least the best I can tell. The fiberglass that caught my eye is in great shape, though the tiny windscreen is cracked in two places. The seller seemed to have owned it for some years and knew enough to take decent care of it—or so I thought, until I tried to get it running.


This Dandy is powered by a Roland RP-40 engine, which is a simple, carbureted two-stroke. Roland might not be a name you recognize, but these days the company goes by[Subaru](http://hagerty.com/media/tags/subaru/) . After pulling off the bodywork and admiring the quality of the frame (at least, compared to my low expectations), a tickle of starting fluid revealed that the engine not only had compression but spark as well. A splash of premix into the tail-mounted gas tank and a bunch more pulls on the starter yielded … nothing.


What is a new-to-you motorcycle if you don’t have to open the carburetor up? Boring, that’s what.


Pull start brings this 40cc two-stroke to life.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


It’s the cutest little Mikuni carburetor.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This is the “stock” exhaust, but according to old ads, there was an expansion chamber that could be purchased separately.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Especially when the carb is a 12mm Mikuni. It’s adorable. The jets are so small I’m shocked the pilot can flow any fluid at all. The clog was more than just the jets, though, as the petcock attached to the carb was also stopped up with a dark and viscous substance most accurately described as *goo* . When I pulled off the fuel line from off the fuel inlet, I counted to three before any fuel flowed, and for that whole time goo oozed from the small fuel hose. The float bowl was worse, yet after what I would consider a light scrub, everything proved functional, and I saw no corrosion or damage worth noting.


With the carburetor reinstalled, the engine fired up on the first pull. Oh, the joy of an easy victory. I love a hard-fought battle with a restoration project as much as the next guy, if not more, but it is so nice when all the screws come out, undamaged. I didn’t even have to use a whole can of carb cleaner. The jets soaked for however long it took to have a nice chat with the missus in the sun on a surprisingly warm late-fall day near the 45th parallel, and that was that.


I still don’t know what I’m going to do with this thing. It’s fun to look at, and worth a few laughs to try and ride from time to time. It would be a fun winter project to learn a little bodywork on the fairing and paint it to replicate a Dick Mann CR750. Plus, it is a fun addition to my mostly Honda motorcycle “collection.” Also seems like the perfect thing to learn a little fiberglass and finish paintwork on, as the stakes seemingly can’t get lower—I got into this little beast for just $150— and I’ve never tried spraying a multi-color paint scheme. I’d like to paint one on my next project in a few years, so learning the tools and techniques on the small scale seems smart.


Those cracks are likely unfixable, but maybe making a new windscreen would be fun?


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This CR750 replica passed through my shop a few years ago, but I think I might borrow the paint scheme.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The Dandy tucked under the footpeg of my KTM 950 Adventure S, for scale.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Display is likely the best idea for the Dandy, at this point in its life. Back when it was new, it might have seen track time, as some motorcycling legends got their[start on pocket bikes](https://youtu.be/1CNd6jjImS0?si=X2UURL7hPPXYVki2) . Today, the tires are cracking pretty badly and were not happy to be inflated for what seems to be the first time in the better part of a decade. More importantly, the top triple clamp that holds the right fork leg is broken. It’s a nifty cast aluminum piece with DANDY, in raised letters, nicely incorporated between the tiny forks. Maybe I’ll upgrade it by making a new billet aluminum triple after learning a few more tricks on a friend’s Bridgeport? Maybe I’ll try to cast a restoration piece?


This bike seems like it will be something fun to work on when I want to, and even when I don’t, it will still be fun to look at. Even something small can teach big lessons. I’m just not sure what those lessons will be yet.
